title: In 66 OpenNeuro task studies, pre-event BOLD state was at most weakly related to reaction time, about one fifth as strongly as the BOLD signal after the event
abstract: The fMRI signal in the seconds before an event was at most weakly related to how fast a person responded to that event, in 66 OpenNeuro task studies with 103 tasks, while the fMRI signal 7-9 s after the event was related to the response time about five times more strongly. This matters because many single studies report that the brain state before a stimulus predicts behaviour, and an earlier study found that the same pre-event signals do not detectably change the evoked response. Data: ReadyNeuro minimally preprocessed BOLD (blood-oxygen-level-dependent) fMRI, one person per study, 25,514 events with a reaction time (RT). Before each event we read the global signal (mean grey-matter BOLD), task-activated cortex, task-deactivated cortex, their balance (deactivated minus activated) and the 30-s global-signal amplitude, after removal of the mean event responses; RT was z-scored log RT within run and trial type. In 36 held-out studies, the positive control (activated cortex 7-9 s after the event) was +0.103 SD of RT per SD (95% CI 0.066 to 0.140). The planned equivalence test (all five pre-event effects inside +-0.035 SD per SD, about 0.8% of RT) passed as frozen; after we corrected errors in public RT columns (clock times, repeated rows, response-locked rows, time-out codes), four measures passed and balance failed (+0.020, 90% CI 0.005 to 0.036). Exploratory and uncorrected, over all studies: lower activated-cortex signal before slower responses, -0.016 SD per SD (p = 0.014; 0.07 after correction for five measures; about 0.4% of RT), same sign in discovery and confirmation; the balance effect is mostly the same signal. In sparse designs (events at least 8 s apart) the pre-event global signal estimate was -0.038 (95% CI -0.069 to -0.006). Lapses, errors and the arousal marker showed no effect. Limits: BOLD-only state, mostly fast designs, one person per study, corrections made after unblinding.

display.caption: Slope of z(log RT) on each BOLD measure (random effects across studies, 90% CI). Grey band: the pre-registered equivalence margin of +-0.035. Above the dashed line: BOLD before the event. Below: BOLD 7-9 s after the event (positive control). Blue: discovery (30 studies); orange: confirmation (36 held-out studies); green: all 66 studies.

Slope of z(log RT) on the BOLD signal read at single 1-s frames from 20 s before to 15 s after event onset, 95% CI. Grey: the 3-s pre-event window. Before the event the slopes are small and mostly negative; after the event the activated cortex and the global signal carry a strong link 6-11 s after onset.
Per-study slopes (95% CI): pre-event global signal (blue) and post-event activated cortex (orange), 66 studies sorted by the post-event slope.

citations.reason: Campaign branch A4 (the condition), leaf prestim-state.

We use its events survey of the ReadyNeuro subset to find runs with reaction times. It found no detectable effect of pre-event BOLD on evoked size; we test behaviour as the outcome, with a positive control in the same runs.
OpenNeuro, source of the BOLD data and events files.
Fox et al. 2006: spontaneous activity and trial-to-trial variability of evoked responses.
Fox et al. 2007: intrinsic fluctuations and behavioural variability (somatomotor cortex, button force).
Weissman et al. 2006: lower pre-stimulus activity in control regions before lapses; our small exploratory effect of task-activated cortex has the same direction.
Goodale et al. 2021: fMRI alertness index before trials predicts behaviour.
He 2013: negative interaction of spontaneous and evoked activity.
Huang et al. 2017: non-additive interaction of spontaneous and evoked activity.
Esterman et al. 2013: attention fluctuations, RT variability and default-mode activity.
Yarkoni et al. 2009: post-event BOLD and trial RT in five studies; our positive control shows this link across 65 studies.
Chang et al. 2016: fMRI arousal fluctuations.
Mayhew et al. 2016: global modulation of single-trial fMRI responses.
